q: You want to dry out against the harbour wall to scrub the hull, and you need the lowest low waters of the fortnight. Which days do you pick?
a: Monday–Tuesday, a day or two after full moon
o: The following Sunday, at the last quarter
Friday–Saturday, just before the full moon
why: Springs, with the lowest LWs, come a day or two after new and full moon; neaps follow the quarters.

q: This morning's high water was at 0640. You plan to cross the bar on the next high water. About when is it?
a: About 1905
why: Semi-diurnal tides: two HWs a day about 12 h 25 min apart. 0640 + 12:25 = 1905.

fig.title: Tide table
lines: No table aboard for later today

q: Springs are today. You want the weakest streams for a passage through the Chenal du Four with an inexperienced crew. When is the best window in the coming fortnight?
a: In about 7 days, at neaps
o: In about 14 days, when the cycle repeats
In about 3 days, as the range falls
In about 11 days, before the new moon
why: Springs to neaps is about 7 days, half the ~14.8-day cycle; neap streams run at roughly half the springs rate.

q: You want the lowest low water of the year to scrub on a drying grid. Why does the almanac show bigger spring ranges in March than in June?
a: Equinoctial springs — sun and moon near the equator
o: Winter gales push extra water into the Channel
The moon is always nearest the earth in March
Low winter pressure deepens every tidal range
why: Near the equinoxes the sun and moon both lie over the equator: equinoctial springs bring the year's largest ranges.

fig.title: Almanac — spring ranges
lines: Plan: scrub on a drying grid at LW

q: The chart shows 1.8 m where you plan to anchor, and the title panel says soundings are reduced to LAT. With ordinary weather, how often will you find less water than that?
a: Hardly ever — LAT is the lowest predicted tide
o: At every low water, twice a day
why: Chart datum is about LAT: predicted tides almost never fall below it; only high pressure or offshore winds take it lower.

q: You plan to spend the night over a charted 1.5 m patch with the low water near springs. What depth do you expect at an average spring low water?
a: 2.2 m — 0.4 m under the keel
o: 0.8 m — you dry out at low water
why: Depth = charted depth + height of tide: 1.5 + MLWS 0.7 = 2.2 m; minus 1.8 m draft leaves 0.4 m.

q: You have today's tide table for the port and the almanac's mean levels. Is today nearer springs or neaps?
a: Neaps — 2.4 m range, close to the 2.2 m neap range
o: Springs — HW 4.2 m is close to the spring HW
Midway — 2.4 m is half the 4.7 m spring range
Springs — 2.4 m is above the 2.2 m neap range
why: Compare ranges: today 4.2 − 1.8 = 2.4 m; springs 5.4 − 0.7 = 4.7 m; neaps 4.1 − 1.9 = 2.2 m. Near neaps.

q: You are in Saint-Malo, and the almanac gives these times and heights for today. What is the range of this morning's flood?
why: Range = HW − LW of the same tide: 9.8 − 1.1 = 8.7 m.

q: You are at anchor waiting for the flood. What is the height of tide at 0600?
why: Range 4.8 m. After 3 h the tide has risen 1 + 2 + 3 = 6/12: 1.0 + 2.4 = 3.4 m.

q: You leave the marina at 1320 on the ebb. What height of tide do you have at that time?
why: Range 4.8 m. Two hours after HW it has fallen 1 + 2 = 3/12 = 1.2 m: 5.4 − 1.2 = 4.2 m.

q: You are over the charted 1.4 m sounding at 0800. Using the rule of twelfths, what depth of water is there?
You have dried out on a sandbank and want to float off as early as possible. In which hours of the flood does the water rise fastest?
a: 0800–1000, the third and fourth hours
o: Evenly — the same amount each hour
why: Rule of twelfths 1-2-3-3-2-1: the 3rd and 4th hours each bring 3/12 of the range.

fig.title: Aground on the sand
lines: Keel in soft sand, no swell

q: You are anchoring over the charted 3.2 m sounding. What depth of water do you expect from the surface to the seabed?
why: Depth of water = charted depth + height of tide: 3.2 + 2.5 = 5.7 m.

q: The short cut to the harbour crosses the bank with the underlined 1.8. How much water is over the bank now?
a: 1.2 m — less than your 1.5 m draft
why: An underlined figure is a drying height above datum: water over it = 3.0 − 1.8 = 1.2 m, less than 1.5 m.

q: You want to cross the bank with the underlined 1.2 and keep 0.5 m under the keel. By the rule of twelfths, what is the earliest time on the flood?
why: Need 1.2 + 1.2 + 0.5 = 2.9 m of tide. Three hours after LW: 0.5 + 6/12 × 4.8 = 2.9 m — at 1000.

q: You are leaving over the bar, charted 0.8 m, on the ebb and want 0.6 m under the keel. By the rule of twelfths, what is the latest time to cross?
The marina sill dries 2.0 m above chart datum. How much water is over the sill now, and what is left under the keel?
a: 2.1 m over the sill, 0.3 m under the keel
o: 6.1 m over the sill, 4.3 m under the keel
4.1 m over the sill, 2.3 m under the keel
2.3 m over the sill, 0.5 m under the keel
why: Water over the sill = 4.1 − 2.0 = 2.1 m; minus the 1.8 m draft leaves 0.3 m. Tight: most skippers want 0.5 m or more.

q: You want 0.6 m under the keel crossing the marina sill on the flood. Using the port's tidal curve, what is the earliest time?
Using the port's tidal curve, what is the height of tide at 1400?
why: Height = LW + range × factor = 1.0 + 4.0 × 0.70 = 3.8 m.

q: You need the height of tide two hours before LW to enter a shallow creek, and your crew has worked it by the rule of twelfths. What do you do?
a: Read it off the port's own tidal curve
o: Accept it — the rule works for every port
Add 10% to the answer to be safe
Use the mean of the HW and LW heights
why: The rule of twelfths assumes a symmetrical 6-hour tide. With a double HW or a stand, use the port's curve.

fig.title: Almanac — Solent port
lines: Rise about 7 h, fall about 5 h

q: You are lying to a buoy where the charted depth is 1.8 m. What depth will you have at this morning's low water?
a: 1.6 m — 0.1 m less than your draft
why: A minus height means the tide falls below chart datum: 1.8 + (−0.2) = 1.6 m, under your 1.7 m draft.

fig.title: Tide table
lines: Charted depth at the buoy 1.8 m

q: You are bound for the secondary port. What are the time and height of its high water?
why: Apply the differences with their signs: 0912 − 0035 = 0837; 5.8 − 0.6 = 5.2 m.

q: You will use the rule of twelfths at the secondary port this afternoon. What range do you work with?
why: Correct both heights first: HW 4.9 + 0.4 = 5.3 m, LW 0.9 + 0.1 = 1.0 m; range 4.3 m.

fig.title: Secondary port
lines: Standard port: HW 4.9 m · LW 0.9 m
Height diff: HW +0.4 m · LW +0.1 m

q: Interpolate the height difference for today. What are the time and height of HW at the secondary port?
why: 5.5 m is halfway from MHWN to MHWS, so the difference is +0.6: 6.1 m. Time 1020 − 0030 = 0950.

q: You need the height of tide at the secondary port at 1500. By the rule of twelfths, what is it?
why: Secondary HW 1300 4.8 m, LW 1900 0.8 m, range 4.0 m. At HW+2 it has fallen 3/12 = 1.0 m: 3.8 m.

fig.title: Secondary port
lines: Diff: HW and LW heights −0.2 m

q: It is HW−1 at the reference port and today is a spring tide. What stream do you plot from the diamond's table?
a: Set 045°T, rate 2.4 kn
why: Read the HW−1 row and the springs column: the stream sets towards 045°T at 2.4 kn.

q: You are about to plot the stream for your EP. Which row of the diamond's table covers the time now?
a: HW+3 — 1415 is 2 h 45 min after HW
o: HW+2 — round down to the whole hour
HW−3 — count to the next high water
why: 1415 is HW+2h45. Each row covers half an hour either side of its hour, so HW+3 (HW+2h30 to HW+3h30).

q: The diamond gives the spring and neap rates for the hour. What rate do you use for today's stream?
a: 2.5 kn

q: You are working up an EP and need the stream at diamond D for the time now. What do you plot?
a: 080°T at 1.7 kn
why: 1140 is HW+2h35, so the HW+3 row. Today is halfway from neaps to springs: 1.0 + 0.5 × 1.4 = 1.7 kn, setting 080°T.

q: You are reading the tidal stream atlas for the next hour and today is a neap tide. What stream do you take from the page?
a: East-going at 0.6 kn
why: Atlas figures give neaps,springs in tenths of a knot: 06,12 is 0.6 kn at neaps and 1.2 kn at springs.

q: You will reach the headland at 1100 and want the stream there from the atlas. Which page do you open?
a: HW−3 — 2 h 40 min before HW Dover
o: HW−1 — 1 h 15 min before local HW
HW+3 — 2 h 40 min after HW Dover
HW−2 — rounded down to whole hours
why: Count from the atlas's own reference port: 1100 is 2 h 40 min before HW Dover, so the HW−3 page.

fig.title: Atlas and tide times
lines: Atlas pages: hours from HW Dover

q: You are motoring north through the sound against the foul stream. Where do you expect the weakest stream?
a: Near the edges, out of the mid-channel stream
o: In mid-channel, where the water is deepest
In the narrowest part of the sound
Off the points at each end of the sound
why: Streams run hardest in the deep middle of a channel, in the narrows and off points; friction slows them at the edges.

q: You are beating west along the coast against a 2 kn foul stream, and the pilot book mentions an eddy in the bay. Where do you sail?
a: Close inshore across the bay, in the eddy
o: Well offshore, where the stream is weaker
On the rhumb line between the headlands
In mid-bay, clear of both shores
why: Bays often hold an eddy or a counter-current inshore; the main stream runs strongest offshore and off the headlands.

q: You are heading west and plan to round the headland while the spring stream runs west against the westerly F6. What do you do?
a: Wait for slack water before rounding
o: Go now, while the stream is fair for you
Round close along the edge of the overfalls
Motor straight through at full speed
why: Wind against a spring stream off a headland raises steep, breaking overfalls. Round at slack, or well outside them.

q: You are crossing the channel today. When do you expect the steepest, most uncomfortable sea?
a: 1700–2300, with the stream against the wind
o: 1100–1700, with the stream and wind together
At 1700, while the stream is slack
All day the same — only the wind matters
why: A SW wind blows towards the NE; the SW-going stream runs into it. Wind against tide shortens and steepens the waves.

q: You are heading SW through the race with a family crew. The stream is fair for you from 0900. What do you decide?
a: Postpone — wind against a spring stream in the race
o: Go at 0900 to carry the fair stream
Go at 1500, once the stream turns foul
Go now and motor-sail hard through it
why: A SW F6 against the spring SW-going stream makes the race dangerous: here a fair stream means wind against tide.

fig.title: Race passage plan
lines: Pilot book: dangerous in wind v tide

q: You want to arrive at the headland just as the stream there turns fair. When do you leave?
why: Fair from HW Dover −1 = 0930; 12 M at 6 kn takes 2 h, so leave at 0730.

fig.title: Tidal gate
lines: Fair stream there from HW Dover −1

q: You are waiting to pass under the bridge on the ebb with your margin. By the rule of twelfths, what is the earliest time?
why: Clearance = 11.5 + 4.8 − height; you need 13.6 m, so height ≤ 2.7 m. HW+3: 5.1 − 6/12 × 4.8 = 2.7 m at 1200.

q: You are motoring up the river towards the bridge. Can you pass under it now, and with how much room?
a: Yes — 14.8 m clearance, 1.0 m to spare
o: No — 12.0 m is less than your 13.8 m
Yes — 20.8 m clearance, 7.0 m to spare
why: Clearance now = charted 12.0 + (HAT 5.8 − tide 3.0) = 14.8 m: 1.0 m over your 13.8 m air draught.

q: The chart gives 9.5 m under the bridge, and your air draught is 9.0 m. What does the 9.5 m tell you about the room under it?
a: At least 9.5 m at almost any state of tide
o: Exactly 9.5 m at every high water
9.5 m at chart datum, less at high water
9.5 m only at mean high water springs
why: HAT is the highest predicted tide, so the real clearance is 9.5 m or more, except in a surge.

q: You need to pass under the power cable across the channel. Can you pass under it now?
a: Yes — 21.0 m clearance, 2.8 m to spare
o: No — 18.2 m tops the charted 18 m
Yes — 18 m clears the 17.2 m mast
why: Safe clearance is above HAT: 18 + (5.0 − 2.0) = 21.0 m. Count the aerial: 18.2 m, so 2.8 m to spare.

q: You are about to drop anchor here for the night. Will you stay afloat at low water?
a: No — 1.4 m at LW, under your draft
o: Yes — 5.0 m now, and it is near HW
why: The tide will drop 4.6 − 1.0 = 3.6 m: 5.0 − 3.6 = 1.4 m at LW, less than the 1.7 m draft.

q: You want 1.0 m under the keel at low water. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the least depth you should anchor in now?
You are off the bar at low water with a swell running. The bar's charted depth is 1.4 m. Do you cross?
a: No — about 1.6 m in the troughs, under your draft
o: Yes — 2.2 m gives 0.4 m under the keel
Yes — the crests add 0.6 m of water
Yes — 3.4 m of water with the swell
why: Depth 1.4 + 0.8 = 2.2 m, but the boat drops about half the 1.2 m swell in a trough: 1.6 m. Wait for the flood.

q: You are about to cross the bar at low water after a week of settled weather. What depth do you allow for on the bar?
a: About 1.8 m
why: 20 hPa above 1013 lowers the sea about 0.2 m: 1.6 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 1.8 m.

fig.title: Before crossing the bar
lines: Charted depth on the bar 1.6 m
Rule: about 1 cm per hPa from 1013

q: You plan to pass under a bridge near high water tonight, with 0.6 m of margin at the predicted height. What do you expect?
a: A higher HW than predicted — the margin may go
o: A lower HW than predicted — more room
The predicted HW — the tables allow for weather
A higher LW only — the HW is unchanged
why: Onshore gales and low pressure (982 hPa, about +0.3 m) pile water up: a surge lifts HW above the tables.

fig.title: Bristol Channel, springs
lines: SW gale F8 for two days
Bridge margin at predicted HW: 0.6 m

q: You are lying on a mooring in a shallow harbour, and the wind has blown hard off the land for three days. What do you expect at low water?
a: Less water than predicted — you may touch
o: More water than predicted — the wind holds it in
The predicted depth — the tables include weather
Less water only at neaps, not at springs
why: Offshore winds and high pressure lower the sea below the prediction; a 0.3 m margin can disappear.

fig.title: Before the morning LW
lines: Strong E wind, offshore, for 3 days
Your margin at predicted LW: 0.3 m

q: You are in the north of the Adriatic, used to tideless Greek harbours, and moor stern-to for the night. Can you ignore the tide at this quay?
a: No — about 1.7 m at LW, under your draft
o: Yes — Mediterranean tides are too small
Yes — charted depths are always at LW
No — about 2.7 m at LW, the tide adds
why: Ranges here are near 1 m; with depths from mean sea level, LW is about 0.5 m lower: 2.2 − 0.5 = 1.7 m.

fig.title: Northern Adriatic quay
lines: Pilot book: spring range about 1 m

q: You have sailed from the Ionian to the Gulf of Gabès and anchored at high water on a wide shallow bank. What do you expect at low water?
a: Aground — the depth falls by about 2 m
o: Afloat — the drop is only about 0.2 m
Afloat — the bank dries only in a gale
why: The Gulf of Gabès has the Mediterranean's largest tides, up to about 2 m at springs: 2.5 − 2.0 = 0.5 m.

fig.title: Gulf of Gabès, Tunisia
lines: Almanac: spring range here up to 2 m
Anchored at HW in 2.5 m · draft 1.9 m

q: You are in a shallow Ionian harbour with little water under the keel, and a deep low is coming. What will change the water level most over the next day?
a: The weather — the pressure and the wind
o: The tide — its 0.2 m range twice a day
The tide — tonight is the full moon
why: Where the range is 0.2 m, a deep low (about +0.2 m) and a gale's surge or set-down move the level more than the tide.

q: The boatyard up the drying creek can only take you on a big spring high water. Today the moon is at first quarter. When do you book the lift?
a: In about 8–9 days, just after the full moon
o: Today, while the moon is at first quarter
In about 4 days, as the moon waxes
In about 15 days, at the next first quarter
why: First quarter brings neaps; the full moon comes about 7 days later and springs a day or two after it — in about 8–9 days.

q: You went out over the bar on this morning's high water at 1015. You want to come back in on tomorrow morning's high water. About when will it be?
a: About 1105
why: Two tides a day of about 12 h 25 min each: the same HW tomorrow is about 24 h 50 min later — 1015 + 0050 = 1105.

q: You plan to anchor this weekend in a bay with a small margin at low water. The almanac shows the moon at perigee on the day of the full moon. What do you expect of these springs?
a: A bigger range than usual — lower low waters
o: A smaller range — perigee damps the tide
The usual range — perigee makes no difference
Higher low waters — the moon lifts the sea
why: At perigee the moon is nearest and pulls hardest: perigean springs have larger ranges, so LW falls below its mean.

fig.title: Almanac — this weekend
lines: Your margin at mean spring LW: 0.3 m

q: You want to avoid the day when the streams in the sound run hardest this week. Which day is that, from the port's tide table?
a: Friday — the largest range, 5.0 m
o: Thursday — the first HW over 5 m
Sunday — the day after the highest HW
why: Stream rates follow the range, not the HW height: Friday 5.5 − 0.5 = 5.0 m beats Saturday 5.6 − 0.8 = 4.8 m.

q: You want to take the boat into the creek behind the drying bank at high water. On which tides can you get in with your margin?
a: Springs only — 2.6 m over the bank, 1.2 m at neaps
o: Neaps only — the stream over the bank is weaker
Springs and neaps — 4.2 m is plenty for 1.5 m
Neither — the bank dries higher than your draft
why: Water over the bank at HW = HW − 3.0: springs 2.6 m (1.1 m under the keel); neaps 1.2 m, less than the 1.5 m draft.

fig.title: The creek over the bank
lines: Draft 1.5 m · want 0.5 m under the keel

q: At neaps you lie here comfortably, with water under the keel at low water. You plan to stay on into springs. What will you have at a spring low water?
a: 0.1 m of water — the keel is on the bottom
o: 1.5 m of water — the same as at neaps
2.3 m of water — springs bring more water
0.9 m of water — the drying height added
why: Water over a drying height = tide − 0.4: neaps 1.9 − 0.4 = 1.5 m; springs 0.5 − 0.4 = 0.1 m — the 1.2 m keel sits on the sand.

q: You plan to lock out of the marina at high water. What time is high water on the ship's clock?
why: The almanac gives UT: add 2 h for French summer time — 1146 + 2 h = 1346.

fig.title: Almanac — Saint-Quay
lines: Ship's clock: French summer time, UT+2

q: You are at anchor waiting for the flood to carry you over the shallows. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the height of tide at 1100?
You are leaving the marina on the ebb and need 3.0 m of tide for the sill. Until what time is there that much?
why: 3.0 m is mid-range, (5.4 + 0.6) ÷ 2, reached at mid-ebb: half of 6 h 30 min after HW — 0800 + 3 h 15 min = 1115.

fig.title: Tide table
lines: Sill: you need 3.0 m of tide

q: You reach the shallow entrance to the anchorage at 1030 on the ebb. Using the rule of twelfths, what height of tide do you expect?
why: First hour 1/12 × 4.8 = 0.4 m; half the second hour, another 1/12 = 0.4 m: 5.6 − 0.8 = 4.8 m.

q: You are working out heights for a day in this port. When is your crew's rule-of-twelfths answer most likely to be wrong?
a: Near HW, while the level hardly changes
o: At mid-flood, in the third and fourth hours
At LW, as the flood begins
Evenly, through every hour of the tide
why: Twelfths assume a smooth, sine-shaped curve; through a long stand the level barely moves, so twelfths overstate the change near HW.

fig.title: Almanac — port notes
lines: Stand of the tide at HW: about 2 h

q: You want to leave over the sill at 1400. Your crew's rule of twelfths says there isn't enough water. Can you go?
a: Yes — the curve gives 5.1 m at 1400
o: No — the twelfths give 4.4 m at 1400
No — the curve gives 4.4 m at 1400
Yes — the twelfths give 5.1 m at 1400
why: Use the curve where there is a stand: 0.8 + 0.90 × 4.8 = 5.1 m, enough for the 4.8 m needed. Twelfths give 5.6 − 1.2 = 4.4 m.

fig.title: Leaving over the sill
lines: Sill: you need 4.8 m of tide

q: Your crew wants a late breakfast before you go. The tide is falling, and you want 0.5 m under the keel over the marina sill. By the rule of twelfths, until when can you still leave?
why: Need 1.8 + 2.1 + 0.5 = 4.4 m of tide. HW+2: 5.6 − 3/12 × 4.8 = 4.4 m — at 1030; then it falls 1.2 m in the next hour.

q: You will cross the bar on the way out at 1600. By the rule of twelfths, what depth will you find over it?
a: 2.9 m — 1.1 m under the keel
why: HW+4: 4.6 − 9/12 × 3.6 = 1.9 m of tide; + 1.0 m charted = 2.9 m, 1.1 m under a 1.8 m keel.

q: Your plan gives 0.3 m under the keel crossing the bar at 2200 on the falling tide, in the dark. What do you do?
a: Cross at 2130 — about 0.5 m under the keel
o: Cross at 2200 — 0.3 m is enough at night
Cross at 2230 — the ebb will have eased
Cross at 2200 — and slow right down on the bar
why: On a falling tide every minute late costs water: half an hour earlier adds 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 m — 0.5 m under the keel.

fig.title: Bar crossing tonight
lines: Ebb · tide falling about 0.4 m an hour
Dark, slight swell on the bar

q: The crew are taking the tender ashore from the anchorage. They need 0.4 m of water at the foot of the slipway to get back off. By the rule of twelfths, when must they be back?

fig.title: Shore trip
lines: Foot of the slipway dries 2.4 m

q: You are working the height of tide from the port's curve diagram, which has a spring and a neap curve. Which curve do you read today?
a: The spring curve — today is close to springs
o: The neap curve — it is the safer, lower one
Halfway between the two, every day
Either — the two curves give the same
why: Today's 5.8 m range is almost the 5.9 m mean spring range: read the spring curve; interpolate only for ranges in between.

fig.title: Tidal curves — standard port
lines: Mean ranges: springs 5.9 m · neaps 2.6 m

q: You are going up river on the flood and must pass under the bridge before the tide gets too high. From the port's curve, what is the latest time?
why: Room = 10.6 + 5.0 − tide must be at least 13.5 m, so tide ≤ 2.1 m: factor (2.1 − 0.8) ÷ 5.0 = 0.26 — HW−4, 0900.

q: You will cross the drying bar of the secondary port at its high water. When is that, and what will you have under the keel?
a: 1120 — 1.2 m under the keel
why: HW there 1140 − 0020 = 1120, 4.8 − 0.4 = 4.4 m; over the bar 4.4 − 1.5 = 2.9 m: 1.2 m under a 1.7 m keel.

q: You are anchored off the secondary port over a charted 1.2 m. When is low water there, and what depth will you have then?

fig.title: Secondary port — LW
lines: Charted depth where you lie 1.2 m

q: You need the time of high water at the secondary port for an early start. Interpolating the time difference, when is it?
You are anchored for lunch over the underlined 0.4 in the bay and want 0.3 m under the keel when you weigh. By the rule of twelfths, what is the latest time to leave?
why: Need 0.4 + 1.5 + 0.3 = 2.2 m of tide. HW+4: 5.8 − 9/12 × 4.8 = 2.2 m — at 1450; after that the spot dries.

q: You anchored at this evening's low water and are happy with the depth. What will you have under the keel at the next low water?
a: 0.2 m — 0.4 m less than tonight
why: Springs are building: the next LW is 0.4 m lower (0.5 v 0.9 m), so 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 m — 0.2 m under a 1.8 m keel.

q: You must pass under the bridge near tonight's high water, and a surge is forecast. How much room will you have?
a: 14.1 m — 0.5 m to spare
why: Room = 14.0 + (HAT 5.6 − HW 5.2 − surge 0.3) = 14.1 m: the surge eats into the HAT margin, leaving 0.5 m over 13.6 m.

q: Your old chart gives the bridge clearance above MHWS. You plan to pass under it at today's high water. Can you?
a: No — 11.6 m at HW, under your 11.8 m
o: Yes — 12.0 m is more than your 11.8 m
why: A clearance above MHWS shrinks when HW tops MHWS: 12.0 − (5.0 − 4.6) = 11.6 m, less than the 11.8 m air draught.

q: Your crew wants to go under the bridge at high water, counting on the high pressure to lower the tide. What do you do?
a: Wait for the ebb to give real room
o: Go — 1038 hPa lowers HW by 0.25 m
Go — the tables already allow for it
why: Pressure effects are rough estimates, not predictions: with no margin at the predicted HW, wait for the falling tide.

fig.title: Bridge at HW
lines: 0.1 m short at the predicted HW

q: You are working up the EP at the end of a two-hour leg, 1100 to 1300, at springs. What total tide vector do you lay off?
why: Lay off each hour: 1.6 M towards 070° (HW+1), then 2.0 M towards 080° (HW+2) — together about 3.6 M towards 076°T.

q: The next two hours of your leg fall in the HW−2 and HW−1 rows of the diamond. How far does the stream carry you over the two hours?
a: 3.7 M towards 255°T
why: Today is midway between neaps and springs: 1.6 + 2.1 = 3.7 M, both hours setting 255°T.

q: You will cross the bay from 1000 to 1200 and take the streams from the atlas. Which two pages do you use?
a: HW, then HW+1
why: Each page covers the hour centred on its time: 1030 is 20 min before HW Dover (the HW page), 1130 is 40 min after (HW+1).

q: You are reading the tidal stream atlas for your next hour. What rate do you use today?
a: 1.8 kn
why: 10,22 means 1.0 kn at neaps, 2.2 kn at springs. Today is 2/3 of the way from neaps to springs: 1.0 + 2/3 × 1.2 = 1.8 kn.

fig.title: Tidal stream atlas
lines: Ranges: sp 5.4 m · np 2.4 m · today 4.4 m

q: Today's range is bigger than the mean spring range. What rate do you use for the stream at the diamond?
a: 3.3 kn
why: Extend the line past springs: 3.0 + (5.6 − 5.0) ÷ 3.0 × 1.6 = 3.3 kn. Capping it at 3.0 kn underestimates it.

fig.title: Equinoctial springs
lines: Mean ranges: sp 5.0 m · np 2.0 m

q: You are plotting the stream at the diamond for the time now. Which row of the table do you use?
a: HW−5 — 5 h 25 min before the 1635 HW
o: HW+6 — the last row after the 0410 HW
why: 1110 is 7 h after the 0410 HW, past the last row: count back from the next HW — 5 h 25 min before 1635 is the HW−5 row.

q: You see these two arrows off the harbour entrance on the chart. What does the feathered arrow tell you?
a: The flood stream, 2.5 kn at springs
o: The ebb stream, 2.5 kn at springs
The flood stream, 2.5 kn at neaps
A current of 2.5 kn at all times
why: On the chart a feathered arrow is the flood stream and a plain one the ebb; the rate shown is the mean spring rate.

fig.title: Chart — stream arrows
lines: Arrow with a feathered tail: 2.5 kn
Plain arrow, the other way: 2 kn

q: You want to cross the race off the point at slack water. From the diamond beside it, about when do you go?
a: About 1240
why: The rate falls to 0.1 kn at HW+3 before the set reverses: HW Dover 0940 + 3 h = about 1240.

q: You want to leave harbour just as the stream outside turns west in your favour. When do you go?
a: About 1530
why: Local HW 1130 is HW Dover −3, so HW Dover is 1430; the stream turns at HW Dover +1 — 1530, four hours after local HW.

fig.title: Leaving harbour
lines: Stream outside turns W-going: HW Dover +1

q: You are beating west along the coast against the last of the foul stream. Where does the stream turn fair first?
a: Close inshore, in the shallower water
o: Offshore, where the stream is strongest
Everywhere at once, at local HW
Off the headlands, where it runs fastest
why: The stream turns earlier close inshore, where it is weaker and the water shallower, than out in the offing.

q: You are motoring up the winding river against the ebb. Where do you steer through each bend?
a: The inside of the bend, out of the main stream
o: The outside of the bend, in the deepest water
Mid-river, on the line of the channel
why: The stream runs hardest round the outside of a bend, where the water is deepest; it is weaker on the inside, depth permitting.

q: Your Mediterranean passage plan takes you north through the strait under motor. What do you time the passage by?
a: The strait's streams — go with the north-going one
o: Nothing — Mediterranean tides are too small
The wind only — the streams follow the wind
Night — the streams are weakest after dark
why: The range there is small, but the streams through the narrows run to about 3 kn: time the passage for the north-going stream.

fig.title: Strait of Messina
lines: Pilot book: streams up to about 3 kn
Your speed under motor 5 kn, bound N

q: You are moored stern-to on a low quay at the north end of the Adriatic, and a two-day Sirocco is forecast. What do you expect of the water level?
a: Higher than predicted — watch the lines
o: Lower than predicted — the wind blows it out
As predicted — the tide here is too small
Lower than predicted — the low pressure
why: A SE Sirocco piles water into the closed north end of the Adriatic, and the falling barometer adds more: expect well above predictions.

fig.title: North Adriatic, Sirocco
lines: Forecast: SE F7 for two days
Moored stern-to on a low quay

q: Your old boat barely out-motors the foul stream off the point. When do you leave for it?
a: 1030 — reach the point as it turns fair
o: 0930 — reach the point an hour early
1430 — leave as the point turns fair
1230 — leave two hours before the turn
why: 18 M at 4.5 kn = 4 h: leave at 1030 to arrive at 1430. An hour early you would make about 0.5 kn against the 4 kn stream.

fig.title: Tidal gate — slow boat
lines: Point 18 M ahead · your speed 4.5 kn
Little stream on the way there
At the point: foul 4 kn until 1430

q: You are heading up the channel to the harbour, and the crew wants to wait at anchor for the fair stream. What do you decide?
a: Go now — you arrive about 40 min sooner
o: Wait 2 h — you arrive about 40 min sooner
Wait 2 h — the foul stream halves your speed
Go now — you arrive about 2 h sooner
why: Now: 5 M in 2 h, then 7 M at 7.5 kn = 56 min — 2 h 56. Waiting: 2 h + 12 M at 7.5 kn = 3 h 36.

fig.title: Up the channel to harbour
lines: Now: foul stream 2.5 kn for 2 h
Crew: “wait 2 h for the fair tide”

q: You plan to cross the bar at tomorrow morning's spring low water. What depth do you really expect on it?
a: About 1.5 m — you would touch
o: About 1.9 m — 0.3 m under the keel
About 2.3 m — the weather adds water
About 1.8 m — only the pressure counts
why: 1.6 + 0.3 = 1.9 m predicted; −0.1 m for 1023 hPa, −0.3 m of set-down: about 1.5 m, under the 1.6 m draft.

fig.title: Spring LW tomorrow
lines: Predicted LW 0.3 m · bar charted 1.6 m
Offshore gale for 2 days: set-down 0.3 m

q: You are drying out your catamaran on the sand over the underlined 1.8 for a scrub. By the rule of twelfths, when do both keels take the ground?
why: She grounds when the tide = 1.8 + 1.1 = 2.9 m. HW+3: 5.3 − 6/12 × 4.8 = 2.9 m — at 1200.

q: You want to dry out your catamaran to scrub both hulls at low water. Where do you put her?
a: On level, firm sand — both keels land together
o: Against the harbour wall, a line from the mast
On soft mud, so the keels sink in gently
On the sloping beach, bows up the slope
why: A catamaran stands on her own keels: choose firm, level ground clear of rocks so she settles evenly — no wall or legs needed.

fig.title: Drying out a catamaran
lines: Plan: scrub both hulls at LW
Spots: the harbour wall, sand, soft mud

q: You are rounding the headland at 0200 with a fair spring stream, and the pilot book warns that it sets onto the point. How do you pass?
a: Well off, outside the overfalls, fixing often
o: Close in to the point, inside the overfalls
Straight for the light, then turn away late
On the plotter track, keeping the speed up
why: At night you can't see the race or judge the set: give the point a wide berth and fix often, as the stream speeds up round it.

q: You are approaching the river bar from seaward with an onshore swell running. When do you cross it?
a: Late in the flood, before HW at 1420
o: Early in the ebb, just after HW at 1420
At LW, once the ebb has finished
Any time — the swell decides, not the stream
why: The ebb running out against an onshore swell makes the bar steep and breaking; cross on the last of the flood, with the most water.

fig.title: River bar, W swell
lines: Onshore swell 1.5 m · wind W F5
Ebb runs out over the bar at 3 kn

q: Your EP is in the bay, close to diamond B; diamond A is out in the main channel. Which stream do you use?
a: B — the nearer, in the same water as you
o: A — the main channel's stream is stronger
The mean of A and B, to be safe
Neither — a bay has no tidal stream
why: Use the diamond nearest you and in the same kind of water; average two only when they are about equally near.

fig.note: Diamonds A and B · depths in metres

q: In fog you are following the 5 m contour into the bay by echo sounder. What reading keeps you on it?
why: Depth over the 5 m contour = 5.0 + 2.3 = 7.3 m; the sounder reads below the keel: 7.3 − 1.8 = 5.5 m.

q: You are alongside a quay wall in a big-tide harbour, with your lines led up to the bollards. How much will the level fall in the next hour?
why: 1100–1200 is the fourth hour of the ebb: 3/12 of the 6.0 m range, 1.5 m — the lines need easing as she drops.

fig.title: Alongside the wall
lines: Lines led up to bollards on the quay

q: You are using an old chart of a quiet anchorage, and tomorrow brings a big spring low water. What may you find there?
a: Less water than the chart shows
o: Never less than the charted depth
why: MLWS is a mean, not the lowest level: a big spring LW falls below it, so you can find less than charted. Modern charts use LAT.
